title: Sensitivities and "what if" questions
objectives: Answer out loud: What happens to the DCF if WACC rises 1%?
Answer out loud: If CapEx rises $10?

steps.body: Build tables that vary two key inputs: WACC vs. terminal growth, WACC vs. exit multiple, revenue growth vs. margin.
The range matters more than any single point estimate.

blocks.template: If terminal growth increases, DCF value {{1}}

blocks.title: Which has a bigger impact: +1% WACC or +1% terminal growth?
blocks.body:
Usually WACC. It affects every discount factor *and* the TV denominator. g only affects the TV. (They're roughly symmetric in the TV denominator, but WACC also discounts every projected year.)

**Interview answer:** "WACC, because it hits every discount factor as well as terminal value, while growth only changes terminal value."

blocks.prompt: Which usually moves a DCF more: +1% WACC or +1% terminal growth?

options.text: +1% terminal growth, because TV is most of the value
+1% WACC, because it hits every discount factor and the TV denominator
Neither — sensitivities only matter for the exit multiple

blocks.explanation: WACC affects every projected year's discount factor as well as the TV denominator; growth only affects TV.

blocks.title: D&A increases by $10 in every year. What happens to the DCF?
blocks.teaser: UFCF rises by the tax shield ($10 × t) each year, since D&A reduces taxable EBIT but is added back.
blocks.body: UFCF rises by the tax shield ($10 × t) each year, since D&A reduces taxable EBIT but is added back. With perpetuity growth TV, value rises further (higher final UFCF). With exit-multiple TV on EBITDA, the TV is unchanged (EBITDA isn't affected). In reality, higher D&A usually comes from higher CapEx, which would lower value.

blocks.title: CapEx increases by $10 a year.
blocks.teaser: UFCF falls by $10 a year; value falls.
blocks.body: UFCF falls by $10 a year; value falls. If the CapEx funds growth, revenue projections should rise too — always ask whether assumptions are consistent.

blocks.title: The tax rate rises.
blocks.body: NOPAT and UFCF fall. The after-tax cost of debt also falls (a larger tax shield), lowering WACC slightly. Net effect: usually value falls.

blocks.title: Why present sensitivity tables at all?
blocks.teaser: The DCF is only as good as its assumptions.
blocks.body: The DCF is only as good as its assumptions. Showing a range across plausible inputs is more honest and shows which assumptions drive value.

prompts: What happens to the DCF if WACC rises 1%?
